SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses
Components of a Compliance Strategy Document

content_blocks.text: View PDF
Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: A commodity/service strategy should not be confused with a Procurement Strategy.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Further information on Procurement Strategy requirements can be found in the Additional Resources.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: A commodity/service strategy is effectively a purchasing plan for a particular good or service i.e. it documents your sourcing strategy.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Key components of a commodity/service strategy with the suggested minimum requirements are included in the document section below.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Further information on Procurement Strategy requirements can be found in the Additional Resources dropdown.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Main Subject of the Contract
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: If your procurement includes both goods and services your approach should be determined by the main subject of the contract. For example if the services/goods subject split is 60%/40% respectively by estimated value then the entire exercise should be treated as a services procurement exercise.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: If your contract consists:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: partly of services and partly of goods
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: partly of social services (or other specific services listed in schedule 3 to The Public Contracts (Scotland) Regulations 2015) and partly of other services,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: then the main subject of the contract is determined by which of the services or goods has the highest estimated value.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: (Please note: the Procurement Journey does not cover procurements which are works contracts or contracts that include ‘utility’ activities e.g. running tramways. This includes works/utilities contracts whose elements:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: cannot be separated or
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: which can be separated but are the main subject-matter of the contract).
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Care and Support Services
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: P lease consider Strategic and Public Social Partnerships; further information is provided below.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: A dditional guidance on determining the type and duration of the contract, and on transitional arrangements can be found in the Care and Support Services Contract Type, Duration and Transitional Arrangements .
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Conflicts of Interest and Fraud
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: As with other stages of a procurement exercise, you must consider conflicts of interest and fraud as part of the Commodity/service strategy stage. This must be in line with relevant procurement legislation and your Organisation’s own governance procedures.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: You must ensure that you take all appropriate measures to prevent, identify and remedy conflicts of interest. You must include measures to combat fraud throughout your procurement exercise.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Strategic Partnerships
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Your Organisation may seek a long-term strategic partner or partners e.g. for a period of 10 or 20 years. This may be to redesign and achieve major changes in service delivery and/or the use of resources.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: For example, your Organisation may work with a supplier(s) to determine what range of services could be provided within available resources. This would be instead of tendering for particular services. In this situation, the choice of strategic partner(s) should be transparent and through a competitive process in accordance with the public procurement rules.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Public Social Partnerships (PSPs)
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: PSPs are strategic partnering arrangements. These are based on a co-planning approach where the public sector can work with third sector organisations. In such cases you would share responsibility for designing services based around service user needs.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: The Scottish Government has published guidance on developing and running Public-Social Partnerships . .
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: A PSP typically comprises three stages:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: third sector organisations work with public purchasers to design a service;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: a consortium of third sector organisations(which may also involve the public sector) conduct a short-term pilot. This helps to refine service delivery limits and maximise community benefits; and
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: if the service is deemed successful, commissioners then consider the most appropriate approach to sustaining the PSP. This could involve a competitive tendering process but other methods of securing service delivery should also be considered.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: You should also consider the current and possible future relationships between the Public Body and the Supplier . You should demonstrate how you intend to develop any relationship with a potential supplier going forward.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Joint Procurement Exercise
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: If you are entering a joint procurement exercise with one or more public sector organisations, you must agree the legal status and requirements of such an exercise at this stage.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: You Organisation may either:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: agree a “lead” authority at this stage. Legally, this lead authority will be the organisation responsible for forming the contract with the successful supplier(s), or
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: enter a truly “joint” exercise. This is where the conduct of the procurement is carried out in the joint name(s) of the participating organisations.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: In either of the above cases, the organisations are jointly responsible for ensuring they comply with all relevant procurement legislation.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Sometimes you could consider having only part of the procurement operating as a joint exercise. In such cases the organisations would be equally responsible for any joint areas. and retain sole responsibility for their own areas.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Other practical areas to consider and plan at this stage include:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: the responsibility for contract management;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: how Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) will be managed and communicated and
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: the reporting / communication network that will be needed between organisations and potential supplier(s)
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: whether a Framework Agreement would be more appropriate than a contract. If so, how would the call offs and management of same be conducted
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: The Strategic Positioning Action Plan
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Having considered the previous points you can identify the position of your commodity/service as either Leverage, Strategic, Routine or Bottleneck. The Strategic Positioning Action Plan provides guidance as to the procurement approach you should adopt in each of these circumstances.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: These suggested approaches provide a starting point on how to proceed with your commodity/service. You must define these further still by looking at your specific commodity/service and the opportunities already identified using the Best Value Triangle.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Best Value Triangle Characteristics
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: There are many characteristics to Best Value that public service organisations are expected to demonstrate. Some relating to procurement are as follows:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Purchase Demand Management Reduce consumption Consolidate spend Improve specification
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Reduce consumption
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Consolidate spend
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Improve specification
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Supply Base Management Restructure relationships Increase competition Restructure supply base
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Restructure relationships
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Increase competition
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Restructure supply base
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Total Cost Management Optimise total supply chain costs Reduce total life cycle / ownership costs Reduce / eliminate transactions
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Optimise total supply chain costs
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Reduce total life cycle / ownership costs
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Reduce / eliminate transactions
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Fair Work Practices
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: In line with Statutory Guidance before starting your procurement you should consider whether Fair Work Practices are relevant and proportionate. If so, you should include a question/questions on Fair Work, to be evaluated along with other relevant criteria. Your question(s) should be informed by the results of your pre-market engagement.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: In line with Statutory Guidance , published under the Act, you should consider including a statement in your strategy outlining your commitment to implementing Fair Work First . The statement should highlight a range of approaches that you may use to promote Fair Work First. That strategy must include a statement on your general policy on the payment of a living wage to those delivering contracts where the value of your regulated contracts in a year will be equal to or greater than £5,000,000.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: By reporting and monitoring the delivery of intended sustainable outcomes, such as Fair Work First, you can more easily demonstrate how you are complying with the Sustainable Procurement Duty.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Organisations must determine if data processing activities are relevant to the commodity/service which is the subject of the procurement exercise.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Organisations must ensure that current and future procurement exercises (including contracts entered into before the legislation came into force) are compliant with GDPR and all relevant procurement documents make reference to the new legislation.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: More detailed information on GDPR can found in Leadership & Governance.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Cyber Risks
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Cyber Risks
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: If the contract will involve, support or rely on the digital processing of information, organisations should ensure that appropriate consideration is given to potential cyber risks and their management.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: Further information on how to assess and manage cyber risks as part of the procurement process can be found in the Scottish public sector Guidance Note on Supplier Cyber Security . Buyers should assess cyber risks and develop minimum cyber security requirements as part of award criteria, if necessary.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy

content_blocks.text: SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Organisations must consider how their procurement processes can facilitate the involvement of SMEs, third sector bodies and supported businesses . These suppliers may have characteristics that give them competitive advantages over larger organisations which may include:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Better levels of service - relative to large bidders, your Organisation's spend will represent a much larger proportion of an SME’s turnover. As a result they may value you more as a customer. You may receive a better and more personal service;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Lower overheads – small bidders' running costs will usually be lower than those associated with larger organisations;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Innovative business solutions - potential for taking a new approach to requirements, e.g. early exploitation of new technology, or providing products or services in new/underdeveloped markets;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Greater flexibility – their size lends them to being able to tailor solutions more effectively, e.g. short management chains and approval routes;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Specialism – many are set up to cater for niche markets which may better match requirements;
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Increased competitiveness in the longer term - rather than limiting competition to a few large bidders (who may be familiar with each other’s operations) inclusion of smaller bidders may lead to an increase in competition.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Compliance Issues and Strategies
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You should consider how you will ensure compliance to the contract.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Compliance is required from all parties throughout the whole Procurement Journey. Governance arrangements, management and budget holder behaviours are key to ensuring compliance.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: The Components of a Compliance Strategy document should encourage maximum uptake of a new contract. Members of the User Intelligence Group (UIG) should champion the contract. Commitment from users should be obtained for the proposed strategy options.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Commodity/Service Strategy Options
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: There will be a number of potential options which are applicable to any commodity/service. These will vary with the type, size and complexity of the requirement.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: In all cases, you should consider a 'Do Nothing' option as a benchmark.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: The Commodity/Service strategy should include a summary of options that clearly details the:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: benefits,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: costs and
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: risks
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: associated with each option. These should demonstrate compliance with any legal obligations. This should help the selection of the required Commodity/Service Strategy option to be pursued in the short, medium and long term.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Estimated benefits within a commodity/service area can be obtained from sources such as:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: benchmarking,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: market testing,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: market trends,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: past discounts and
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: previous experience.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Identification and assessment of “softer” benefits should be undertaken at this stage.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Costs to implement sourcing strategies include:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: contract switching costs,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: supplier switching costs,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: resource investment,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: communications and roll out and
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: cost of going to tender
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: The Options Appraisal summarises the various delivery options, considering the benefits and risks of each before selecting an option for recommendation.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: The recommended option must satisfactorily meet the requirements, be affordable, viable and agreed with the UIG.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Division of Contracts into Lots
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You must consider awarding your contract in separate lots. Division into lots can increase SME participation.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Where you decide not to award a contract in the form of lots, you must indicate the main reasons for not doing so. These reasons must be included in the relevant Procurement Documents, or in the procurement exercise written report .
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Potential reasons for not subdividing contracts into lots may be:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: that it would risk restricting competition,
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: it would make contract execution excessively technically difficult or expensive, or
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: the need to coordinate the different contractors for the lots could seriously risk undermining the proper execution of the contract.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You must state in the relevant Procurement Documents, whether bids may be submitted for one, for several or for all lots. Where more than one lot may be awarded to the same bidder contracts may be awarded that combine several or all lots. You must have specified this can happen and include the groups of lots that may be combined. If you use this approach, you must think carefully about how the relevant evaluation matrices will assess all possible scenarios.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You can limit the number of lots that any one bidder can win. To do so you must state the maximum number of lots per bidder in the relevant Procurement Documents.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Where the application of the award criteria would result in one bidder being awarded more lots than the maximum number of lots per bidder, the Organisation would then apply the objective and non-discriminatory criteria or rules which must be indicated in the relevant Procurement Documents.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Sub-contractors
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: During the Profiling the Commodity stage of your procurement exercise, you should have considered whether bidders may sub-contract any of the awarded works or services. If so, question 4.C.4 from the SPD should be included to be evaluated alongside other criteria at selection stage.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Confirmation of how bidders will ensure payment of sub-contractors at all stages of the supply chain pertaining to the contract, within the standard 30 day payment terms and how this will be managed should be evaluated at award stage.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Contract Implementation/Contract and Supplier Management
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: There are separate stops on the Procurement Journey on Contract Mobilisation and Implementation and Contract and Supplier Management (C&SM).Your approach must be considered during this 'Develop Commodity/Service Strategy' phase.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You must consider how the proposed options will operate throughout the life of the requirement. For example, if you decide to use an existing contract or framework agreement the contract implementation and management will be covered in the framework terms and conditions. These must be complied with in full.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You must think about how the new goods or services will be introduced into your organisation. Also how will you move from your existing arrangements to the new arrangements?
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You should also consider your transition or exit strategy for when this new contract or framework agreement comes to an end.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Once fully operational you should manage and develop the contract and supplier(s) to ensure the contract requirements are met now, and in the future.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You must consider the resources required to implement and manage the contract or framework agreement. A designated contract manager should be identified. Additional guidance can be found in the Planning & Governance station .
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: You should detail the CSM requirements in the contract or framework agreement terms and conditions. This will ensure both parties are clear on their contractual obligations. The contract should then be managed in accordance with these terms and conditions.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: The level of CSM required depends on the risk, value and complexity of the contract. You will find guidance to help assess the potential level management of CSM required in the Contract and Supplier Management / Planning and Governance station.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Generally, "Routine" contracts will require a lower level of management than "Leverage" and "Bottleneck" (medium level), and "Strategic" which will require the highest level.
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: There may be opportunities for your organisation to make its own internal processes more efficient. Some of the key areas to consider during the procurement process are:
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Use of PCS-Tender
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: The transactional procurement process: requisitioning, authorising, raising and sending purchase orders, goods receipting, invoicing and payment
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: Further guidance can be found in the Planning & Governance station .
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses

content_blocks.text: As with all aspects of the Procurement Journey, the activities at this stage must be carried out in a carefully managed manner that supports the Principles of Procurement .
heading_path: Commodity Service Strategy v Procurement Strategy
SMEs, and Third Sector Supported Businesses
